content: Superfluidity represents a unique phase of matter where liquids, such as helium-4 or helium-3, exhibit extraordinary behaviors, including the complete absence of viscosity. This phenomenon occurs when these liquids are cooled to extremely low temperatures, reaching a critical point known as the lambda point in the case of helium-4. At this stage, the liquid transitions into a state where it can flow without any resistance due to friction. This property is a cornerstone of quantum hydrodynamics and was first identified in 1937 by Pyotr Kapitsa, John F. Allen, and Don Misener. The theoretical understanding of superfluidity has been developed through both phenomenological and microscopic approaches. Although the superfluid states of helium-4 and helium-3 share similar macroscopic behaviors, their underlying microscopic mechanisms differ significantly. Helium-4 atoms are bosons, and their superfluidity arises from Bose-Einstein condensation in an interacting system. In contrast, helium-3 atoms are fermions, and their superfluidity is explained by an extension of the BCS (Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer) theory of superconductivity. In helium-3, Cooper pairing occurs between atoms rather than electrons, with the attractive interaction mediated by spin fluctuations instead of phonons. This distinction highlights the fundamental differences in the quantum mechanical behavior of bosons and fermions. Both superconductivity and superfluidity can be described within a unified framework involving the breaking of gauge symmetry. Superfluid helium exhibits a range of remarkable properties. It behaves as if it consists of two components: a normal fluid component with conventional properties and a superfluid component characterized by zero viscosity, zero entropy, and infinite thermal conductivity. This infinite thermal conductivity means that it is impossible to establish a temperature gradient within the superfluid, analogous to the inability to create a voltage difference in a superconductor. One striking manifestation of these properties is the thermomechanical or fountain effect. This behavior is explained by the Clausius-Clapeyron relation. Another unusual property of superfluid helium is its ability to form a thin film, just one atom thick, that climbs the walls of any container it occupies. Additionally, when superfluid helium is placed in a rotating container, it does not rotate uniformly with the container. Instead, it forms quantized vortices. Below a critical rotational velocity, the superfluid remains stationary. Once this critical velocity is exceeded, the superfluid begins to rotate, but only at specific quantized speeds, determined by the quantum mechanical properties of the system. Superfluid helium has found applications in various scientific and technological fields. In chemistry, superfluid helium-4 has been employed as a quantum solvent in a technique known as Superfluid Helium Droplet Spectroscopy (SHeDS). This method allows individual gas molecules solvated in the superfluid to exhibit rotational freedom, mimicking their behavior in the gas phase. Furthermore, superfluids have been utilized to manipulate the speed of light. In a groundbreaking experiment by Lene Hau, light was slowed to just 17 meters per second as it passed through a superfluid, compared to its usual speed of 299,792,458 meters per second in a vacuum. This phenomenon does not alter the fundamental constant of the speed of light (c) but demonstrates the interaction of light with a medium. Superfluid helium has also been used in space exploration, such as in the Infrared Astronomical Satellite (IRAS), which was cooled to 1.6 K (-271.4°C) using 720 liters of superfluid helium. Recent advancements in the study of superfluidity include the creation of a fermionic condensate from pairs of ultra-cold fermionic atoms. Under specific conditions, these fermion pairs form diatomic molecules that undergo Bose-Einstein condensation. At the opposite extreme, fermions, such as superconducting electrons, form Cooper pairs that also exhibit superfluidity. This research has enabled scientists to explore the intermediate region between these two extremes, known as the BEC-BCS crossover. Additionally, in 2004, physicists at Penn State University reported the possible discovery of supersolids.
